title: Monitoring in Production
subtitle: Connect production traces to user outcomes and an operational response
summary: Production monitoring must explain more than whether the agent’s infrastructure is running. Model calls, tool invocations, retries, and user outcomes can fail independently, so traces and logs need shared identifiers and workflow context. The chapter connects instrumentation, log and trace storage, dashboards, and alerting into an operational feedback system. Version information helps distinguish a deployment regression from ordinary variation, while semantic measures reveal misunderstood intent or unhelpful results that uptime cannot show. Useful signals lead to owners and response paths. Product, model, and infrastructure teams need a common view so repeated calls, high cost, or abandonment become actionable service problems.

concepts.title: Monitoring layers
concepts.body: Production monitoring spans infrastructure, agent behavior, tools, outcomes, and user experience. CPU or uptime alone cannot reveal a misunderstood intent or a harmful action.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: The service’s uptime remains normal while order cancellations fail because a tool credential expired. Tool-error and completed-task measures reveal the failure that machine health misses.

concepts.title: Traces and logs
concepts.body: A trace links a request to model invocations, tool calls, latency, and results; logs preserve searchable event detail. Together they make a probabilistic workflow inspectable while respecting data sensitivity.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A shared request identifier links the user’s message, two model calls, and a timed-out shipping lookup. The responder can locate the delay without joining unrelated customer records.

concepts.title: Signal versus noise
concepts.body: Monitoring asks whether intent was understood, the right tool selected, and the result useful. Thresholds and sampling should distinguish true regressions from natural variation to avoid overreaction.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: Morning traffic naturally increases total token consumption, so the team compares cost per completed task and failure rates before treating the higher total as a regression.

concepts.title: Alerts and response
concepts.body: An alert is valuable when it maps to an owner and an action. Dashboards, alerts, and post-incident analysis turn production behavior into learning and feed improvements.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A sustained rise in failed cancellation tool calls alerts the owning team with the affected version and response procedure. A small isolated latency fluctuation remains diagnostic data.

misconceptions.claim: Monitoring layers is provided automatically by a more capable model.
misconceptions.correction: Production monitoring spans infrastructure, agent behavior, tools, outcomes, and user experience. CPU or uptime alone cannot reveal a misunderstood intent or a harmful action.

misconceptions.claim: Traces and logs removes the need for evaluation or human judgment.
misconceptions.correction: A trace links a request to model invocations, tool calls, latency, and results; logs preserve searchable event detail. Together they make a probabilistic workflow inspectable while respecting data sensitivity. Evaluation and appropriate oversight remain necessary.

scenario.title: Production incident visibility
scenario.context: Users report wrong tool choices, but dashboards show healthy CPU and uptime.

options.label: Trace intent, calls, results, and outcomes
options.benefit: Localizes probabilistic failures and gives operators a response path.
options.cost: Instrumentation and sensitive-data controls require effort.
options.consequence: A trace shows retrieval failure rather than model failure, shortening repair time.

options.label: Watch infrastructure only
options.cost: Behavioral regressions remain invisible until escalations grow.
options.consequence: The team repeatedly restarts healthy servers without fixing selection.

scenario.debrief: Both choices can fit different constraints. The decision should state stakes, reversibility, evidence, and who owns correction.

quiz.question: Why correlate model calls and tool calls in one trace?
options: To assume every error came from the model.
To reconstruct the steps and dependencies behind a result.
To replace all user-level quality measures with latency.
quiz.explanation: An end-to-end trace helps distinguish model, tool, orchestration, and dependency failures.

quiz.question: Which alert is more actionable?
options: Every unusual token-count change regardless of impact.
An alert sent only after the team has already fixed the issue.
A consequential failure condition with an owner and a response path.
quiz.explanation: Monitoring should connect signals to decisions rather than create undifferentiated noise.

quiz.question: Why monitor cost alongside task success and latency?
options: A behavior change can preserve answers while making the workflow uneconomic.
Low cost proves the output is correct.
Cost is identical across all tool trajectories.
quiz.explanation: Repeated calls, retries, and longer trajectories can alter operating cost independently of correctness.
